items.stem: A school nurse teaches caregivers after a child is diagnosed with pinworm (enterobiasis). Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Treat the infected child, household members, and caregivers with the same timed medication course as directed.
Wash hands with soap and warm water after toileting, after diaper changes, and before handling food.
Wash clothing, towels, and bedding used by the affected person in hot water and dry on high heat when possible.
Give only one lifetime dose of anthelmintic medication because eggs are also killed permanently by a single dose.
Ignore household contacts because pinworms never spread within families.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: treat infected persons, caretakers, and household members at the same time (two-dose schedule). Merck: multiple household infestations are common; treatment of the entire family may be necessary.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC and Merck: handwashing with soap and warm water after toilet/diapers and before food is the key prevention step.
rationales.C: Correct. CDC: wash clothes/washcloths/towels/bedding in hot water and dry hot. Merck: frequently wash clothing, bedding, and toys.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC: two doses about two weeks apart because medication kills worms but not eggs. Merck: single dose repeated in 2 weeks.
rationales.E: Incorrect. CDC and Merck: household members and caregivers are at increased risk; concurrent treatment/prevention is needed.

items.stem: A public health nurse teaches a family about head lice. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.

rows.text: Head lice spread mainly by direct head-to-head (hair-to-hair) contact
Children diagnosed with head lice must be sent home from school immediately mid-day and kept out until every nit is removed
Avoid sharing hats, combs, brushes, and towels; wash recently used linens and clothing in hot water when possible
Fumigant sprays or fogs are required to disinfect the entire home after any lice case

rationales.R1: Accurate. CDC: most common spread is head-to-head contact. Merck: easily transmitted by close contact in households/classrooms.
rationales.R2: Not accurate. CDC: children need not be sent home early; go home end of day, start treatment, return after treatment begun. Merck cites CDC school guidance.
rationales.R3: Accurate. CDC: do not share hats/combs/brushes/towels; hot-water laundry for recent items. Merck discusses washing/drying hot for personal items.
rationales.R4: Not accurate. CDC: do not use fumigant sprays/fogs — not necessary and can be toxic.

items.stem: A toddler is referred after a caregiver notices a firm swelling in the abdomen. Imaging is consistent with Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Which finding is the most frequent presenting feature of Wilms tumor?

options.text: A painless, palpable abdominal mass
Night sweats with migratory polyarthritis as the sole finding
Painless jaundice from birth without a mass
Isolated petechiae covering the trunk without organomegaly

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: the most frequent finding is a painless, palpable abdominal mass. OpenStax: Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma presents in childhood with kidney enlargement (and often hypertension).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Not the classic primary presentation of Wilms tumor (Merck lists mass as most frequent).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Jaundice is not the most frequent Wilms presentation (Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Petechiae alone are not the characteristic Wilms presentation (Merck).

items.stem: A school-age client newly diagnosed with celiac disease is learning diet teaching. Complete the statements.

ngn.template: Celiac disease is treated with a {B1} diet. The client must avoid gluten proteins found in {B2}.

rationales.B1a: Incorrect. Treatment is lifelong gluten-free diet, not a short-term low-fat diet (OpenStax; Merck).
rationales.B1b: Correct. OpenStax: lifelong strict gluten-free diet. Merck: mucosal changes resolve with a strict gluten-free diet.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Not the celiac diet prescription (OpenStax; Merck).
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Clear liquids are not lifelong celiac therapy (OpenStax; Merck).
rationales.B2a: Correct. Merck: gliadin fraction of gluten in wheat; similar proteins in rye and barley. OpenStax: gluten in wheat, barley, and rye.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Salt is not the gluten source to avoid (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Fresh fruit is not the gluten source requiring lifelong exclusion (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Water is not a gluten grain protein (Merck; OpenStax).

items.stem: An infant younger than 1 year has severe foreign-body airway obstruction (cannot cry effectively, weak cough, cyanosis). Which action is correct?

options.text: Give repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive; do not use abdominal thrusts.
Perform only abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) as the sole first-line method for infants.
Do blind finger sweeps immediately to dig deeply in the mouth before any other action.
Offer the infant a large drink of water to wash the object into the stomach.

rationales.A: Correct. AHA/AAP Pediatric BLS 2025: infants with severe FBAO — cycles of 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts not recommended. Merck: back blows followed by chest thrusts for severe infant choking.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in infants (AHA/AAP; Merck uses chest thrusts for infants).
rationales.C: Incorrect. AHA/AAP: blind finger sweeps should not be performed.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Giving fluids does not relieve severe FBAO and delays effective relief (AHA/AAP; Merck procedure).

items.stem: An 8-month-old suddenly cannot cry, has a weak cough, and looks blue around the lips after playing with a small toy. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, 2 priority actions, and 2 parameters that support severe obstruction.

conditions.text: Mild foreign-body airway obstruction with effective cough
Severe foreign-body airway obstruction in an infant
Simple nasal congestion without airway compromise
Resolved choking with no residual risk

actions.text: Activate emergency response and begin cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 chest thrusts
Perform abdominal thrusts only as first-line infant relief
Allow the infant to keep trying without intervention while severe signs persist
If the infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR beginning with compressions and remove a visible object when opening the airway
Give a bottle of milk to push the object down

parameters.text: Inability to cry or make much sound
Strong, effective coughing with good air movement
Cyanosis or color change with severe obstruction signs
Quiet comfortable play with normal feeding
Afebrile ear tugging without respiratory distress

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Mild FBAO allows effective cough/sounds; this infant cannot cry effectively (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.K2: Correct. Severe infant FBAO: cannot cry effectively, weak cough, cyanosis (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Presentation matches severe FBAO, not simple congestion.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Severe signs are present now.
rationales.A1: Correct. Activate EMS and cycles of 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.A2: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts not recommended in infants (AHA/AAP).
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Severe FBAO requires immediate intervention (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.A4: Correct. If unresponsive, start CPR with compressions; remove visible object when opening airway (AHA/AAP).
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Fluids do not relieve FBAO and delay care.
rationales.P1: Correct. Inability to cry/make sound indicates severe obstruction (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.P2: Incorrect. Strong effective cough suggests mild FBAO — observe rather than force relief maneuvers (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.P3: Correct. Cyanosis/color change is a severe obstruction sign (AHA/AAP; Merck).
rationales.P4: Incorrect. Not consistent with severe FBAO.
rationales.P5: Incorrect. Ear tugging without distress does not identify this airway emergency.

items.stem: A client is hospitalized with invasive meningococcal disease. Which action best protects close contacts?

options.text: Offer recommended antibiotic chemoprophylaxis to close contacts (for example household contacts and others with unprotected exposure to respiratory secretions) as directed by public health/clinician guidance.
Tell household contacts that antibiotics are never used after meningococcal exposure.
Advise casual hallway passersby with no close contact that they all require the same immediate chemoprophylaxis as household members.
Wait until the index client finishes a full month of therapy before considering any contact measures.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: close contacts should receive prophylactic antibiotics. CDC isolation appendix: postexposure chemoprophylaxis for household contacts and HCWs exposed to respiratory secretions.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for close contacts (Merck; CDC).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Prophylaxis targets close contacts/unprotected respiratory exposure, not all casual contacts (Merck; CDC).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Close-contact prophylaxis is timely after exposure; do not delay for a month (Merck; CDC).

items.stem: An older adult is being transferred from hospital to a skilled nursing facility. Which nursing action best reduces medication-related harm during the transition?

options.text: Perform medication reconciliation — identify and communicate an accurate list of current medications (name, dose, frequency, route) and resolve discrepancies at the handoff.
Omit the medication list from the transfer so the receiving nurse can rediscover drugs by trial and error.
Stop all chronic medications without review because hospitalization always eliminates every prior indication.
Rely only on the client's memory for high-alert drug doses and skip verification with the record.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: inadequate communication at care transitions is a major cause of adverse drug effects; medication reconciliation at admission/discharge/other transitions can prevent many problems. AHRQ MATCH toolkit: medication reconciliation at transitions and clinical handoffs.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Omitting the list increases transition errors (Merck; AHRQ).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Ongoing need should be reevaluated, not blindly stopped without reconciliation (Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Reconciliation uses a verified current list, not memory alone (Merck; AHRQ).

items.stem: During a rapid response, the team lead needs to share critical information with everyone at once and assign a named person to act. Which TeamSTEPPS tool fits best?

options.text: Call-out — communicate important or critical information to all team members simultaneously, help them anticipate next steps, and direct responsibility by name to the person accountable for the task.
Remain silent so no one hears vital changes until after the event.
Send only an unsigned sticky note without confirming who will act.
Whisper to one person while others continue unaware of the critical change.

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: a call-out communicates important/critical information, informs all members simultaneously, helps anticipate next steps, and directs responsibility by name. Closed-loop communication uses call-outs (with check-backs/teach-back). OpenStax: TeamSTEPPS is an AHRQ teamwork/communication framework nurses use to enhance performance and safety.
rationales.B: Incorrect. TeamSTEPPS emphasizes timely critical communication (AHRQ).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Call-outs direct accountability to a named individual (AHRQ).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Call-outs inform the whole team simultaneously (AHRQ).

items.stem: An adolescent reports abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus with anorexia and nausea and later settled in the right lower quadrant. Which condition does this classic pattern most strongly suggest?

options.text: Acute appendicitis
Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis alone
Simple tension headache without abdominal findings
Stable healed fracture of a finger

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: classic acute appendicitis — epigastric/periumbilical pain followed by nausea/vomiting/anorexia, then pain shifts to the right lower quadrant. OpenStax: appendicitis presents with right lower quadrant or periumbilical pain; anorexia, nausea, vomiting.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain this abdominal pain pattern.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Headache alone does not match the described abdominal progression.

items.stem: A child is admitted with active head lice infestation requiring inpatient care. Which transmission-based precaution plan is appropriate?

options.text: Contact Precautions plus Standard Precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy.
Airborne infection isolation with N95 for all staff indefinitely, regardless of treatment.
No precautions beyond open cohorting with immunocompromised roommates.
Droplet Precautions only, without considering contact measures for lice.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: Pediculosis (lice) — Contact + Standard until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy. Merck: head lice transmitted by close contact; treat with topical pediculicides.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lice are not managed with indefinite airborne isolation (CDC lists Contact + Standard for pediculosis).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contact Precautions are indicated until 24 hours after effective therapy begins (CDC).
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC specifies Contact + Standard for pediculosis, not Droplet-only.

items.stem: A child is in the PACU after tonsillectomy. Which nursing actions help detect postoperative hemorrhage early? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation for hypotension, tachycardia, or other instability.
Assess the surgical site and dressings/drainage for bleeding, including hidden pooling.
Notify the surgical team promptly if hemorrhage is suspected and prepare for ordered interventions.
Assume bright red continuous bleeding is expected and never reassess the wound.
Skip circulation checks because bleeding never occurs after tonsillectomy.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: PACU nurse monitors for hypotension, shock, and hemorrhage using vital signs/oxygenation. Merck postop: monitor hemodynamic status.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax: frequent wound checks for drainage/pooling reveal bleeding. Merck: check wound for increasing drainage/infection signs.
rationales.C: Correct. OpenStax: if hemorrhaging, notify charge/surgeon/anesthesia and prepare fluids/blood products/possible return to OR.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Continuous bright bleeding requires reassessment and escalation (OpenStax hemorrhage intervention).
rationales.E: Incorrect. Hemorrhage is a key PACU risk to monitor after surgery, including tonsillectomy scenarios (OpenStax).
